content: In countries with a high incidence of tuberculosis (TB) and/or leprosy, neonates in locally identified risk groups for these diseases should be vaccinated with Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG). However, in countries with low TB incidence, BCG vaccination is often replaced by intensified case detection, contact tracing, and supervised early treatment. Studies have shown minimal or no additional benefit from repeat BCG vaccination against TB or leprosy, and therefore revaccination is not recommended, even if the tuberculin skin test (TST) or interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) results are negative. The absence of a BCG scar after vaccination does not indicate a lack of protection and is not a reason for revaccination. For children known to be HIV-infected, BCG vaccination should not be administered due to the increased risk of disseminated BCG disease. However, HIV-infected individuals, including children, who are receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART), are clinically well, and are immunologically stable (CD4 percentage >25% for children under 5 years or CD4 count ≥200 for those over 5 years) may be vaccinated with BCG. In populations with high HIV prevalence, where the burden of TB is also significant, the risks associated with BCG vaccination often outweigh the benefits. In such cases, neonates born to women of unknown HIV status should still be vaccinated, as the benefits of BCG vaccination outweigh the risks. Neonates of unknown HIV status born to HIV-infected women should also be vaccinated if they show no clinical evidence of HIV infection, regardless of whether the mother is receiving ART. For neonates with confirmed HIV infection, BCG vaccination should be delayed until ART has been initiated and the infant is clinically and immunologically stable (CD4 percentage >25%). Household and close contacts of TB patients should be evaluated based on their risk of developing TB or the potential consequences of the disease. Priority should be given to children with TB symptoms, children under 5 years of age, children with known or suspected immunocompromising conditions (especially those living with HIV), and child contacts of index cases with multidrug-resistant (MDR) or extensively drug-resistant (XDR) TB. Contact investigation is recommended for household and close contacts of index cases with sputum smear-positive pulmonary TB, MDR/XDR TB, HIV infection, or children under 5 years of age. In settings with high HIV prevalence, all household and close contacts of TB patients should be counseled and tested for HIV. In settings with low HIV prevalence, household members and close contacts of TB patients with symptoms compatible with TB disease may be offered HIV counseling and testing as part of their clinical evaluation. Children under 5 years of age who are household or close contacts of TB patients and are found not to have TB disease after clinical evaluation should receive six months of isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) at a dose of 10 mg/kg per day (range 7–15 mg/kg, maximum dose 300 mg/day). This recommendation is supported by high-quality evidence. Children aged 5 years and older, adolescents, and adults who are household contacts of bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB cases and are found not to have TB disease may also be offered TB preventive treatment. Recommended regimens for TB infection treatment include six or nine months of daily isoniazid, a three-month regimen of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid, or a three-month regimen of daily isoniazid plus rifampicin. In settings with high TB transmission, adults and adolescents living with HIV who have an unknown or positive TB infection test and are unlikely to have TB disease should receive at least 36 months of daily IPT, regardless of ART status, degree of immunosuppression, history of previous TB treatment, or pregnancy. Children living with HIV who are more than 12 months old, unlikely to have TB disease based on symptom screening, and have no contact with a TB case should be offered six months of IPT as part of comprehensive HIV prevention and care services in high TB prevalence settings. In medium or low TB prevalence settings, they may also be offered six months of IPT. Infants under 12 months of age living with HIV who are in contact with a TB patient and are unlikely to have TB disease should receive TB preventive treatment. Children aged 12 months or older living with HIV who are unlikely to have TB disease should be offered TB preventive treatment as part of comprehensive HIV care, regardless of contact with TB. All children living with HIV who have successfully completed TB treatment may also receive TB preventive treatment. Children with suspected or confirmed pulmonary TB or tuberculous peripheral lymphadenitis living in high HIV prevalence settings (or with confirmed HIV infection) should not be treated with intermittent regimens (e.g., twice-weekly or thrice-weekly dosing). Daily dosing remains the recommended frequency for drug-susceptible pulmonary TB in both the intensive and continuation phases of therapy. Children with proven or suspected pulmonary TB or tuberculous meningitis caused by MDR bacilli can be treated with a fluoroquinolone as part of an appropriate MDR-TB regimen, under the guidance of an experienced clinician. For children with MDR/RR-TB under six years of age, an all-oral treatment regimen containing bedaquiline may be used. For children under three years of age, delamanid may be included in longer MDR-TB regimens. All children treated for TB should be recorded and reported by national tuberculosis programs (NTPs) in specific age bands (e.g., 0–4 years and 5–14 years). Updated age bands for reporting TB in children and adolescents now include 0–4, 5–9, 10–14, and 15–19 years. In children with presumptive pulmonary TB attending healthcare facilities, integrated treatment decision algorithms may be used for diagnosis. In TB high-burden settings, decentralized TB services and family-centered, integrated services may be used for children and adolescents with TB symptoms or those exposed to TB.
